I'm tracing through the pose chain for obs_0164, applying the turn and move commands from f162 through f164 to compute the resulting positions and headings, then checking how that aligns with the mass's north end and west face coordinates.

With no collision reported for the move to (2.050, 7.900), that checks out since the camera clears the mass at that y-coordinate. Then I look at obs_0163's frame, which shows only white wall since the camera is too close to the north wall for anything else to register — an uninformative frame.

Now for obs_0164, I'm parsing the pixel groups: the dark ceiling band, the tan floor strip, and a second cluster of gb regions further along the u-axis, along with two distinct dark color values that might correspond to different shadow depths or surface types, checking whether they satisfy the gb mask threshold.

I'm working through the geometry — figuring out that the east wall's base row in the image shifts with u because the distance to the wall increases off the central viewing axis, so I need to recompute the expected v-position using the angle-dependent distance formula.

Actually the depth Z along the optical axis is constant at the wall for all columns, so v=467 uniformly — I confused myself earlier. So the east wall base sits at v=467 across the whole image.

Comparing to the observed floor transition around v=473 for columns 224–352, that's only about 6 pixels off, which I should check against the camera position assumption.

Testing px=2.10 instead of 2.05 gives a wall distance of x=3.93 and depth Z=1.83, producing v=473 — a much better match, so the actual player position is closer to px≈2.10.

Now I'm puzzling over why the floor tan region only appears for u224–352, and why columns u<224 show no ceiling color at all, which seems inconsistent with a normal room render.

I'm reconsidering the geometry at heading 90 (facing east): image-left corresponds to north, and since camera y=7.9 sits just 0.37m from the north wall at y=8.27, that wall should occupy a specific lateral band on the left side of the frame based on how the receding plane projects.

So the east wall covers u 204–511, matching the floor's tan region starting near u=224, just past the north wall boundary. But for u 0–204, no floor tan appears at all, meaning the north wall's base line dips below v=511 in that range—checking column u=204 gives v≈474, while at u=100 the base drops off screen entirely around v≈910, confirming no floor is visible there.

Now I'm tracking darker structures at u=372–511, rows 415–511, with a mid-gray tone around (76,80,86) and a near-black tone around (22,24,25). The tan floor cuts off past u=352, and scanning across columns—u=372, 400, 420, 460—the pattern shows white extending further right as u increases, followed by the mid-gray band, then the near-black band deeper down, suggesting a receding dark shape or shadow structure in that region.

At u=500 and u=511, the pattern shifts: tan floor reappears briefly around v=480, then transitions into a slightly different gray around (82,86,92). This suggests the dark object's near edge is sloping, starting higher at u=372 and lower toward u=460, but at u=500 there's floor visible before the dark region resumes—implying the object doesn't extend that far right, or its shape curves back at the base.

If I back-project the top edge at v=495 assuming this is a low object sitting on the floor, I can estimate its distance using the standard height-to-depth relationship, and I'm now wondering if this dark region is actually the mass itself rather than a separate obstacle.

Realizing the mass's north face at y=7.44 sits just 0.46 m to my right given my position at (2.10, 7.90), which would place it appearing on the right side of the frame since right corresponds to south in my view. Working out the projection: a point on that north face at depth Z would appear at a horizontal position offset by 256*0.46/Z, and its top edge (z=1.166) would land at v=256+98.3/Z — so I'm now calculating the depth to the mass's northwest corner to pin down exactly where it should appear.

Testing that math, the NW corner ends up projecting off-frame at u=587, which is beyond the 511-pixel edge — so that corner isn't even visible. Trying different points along the top edge of the north face at increasing x-values still doesn't line up with the observed edge near u372, v415, since my calculations put v closer to 365 at comparable positions, so this face orientation doesn't match what's actually visible in the image, and the fact that the observed edge slopes the wrong way makes me suspect I have the geometry or orientation backwards.

I'm starting to think this dark shape isn't the mass top at all, but possibly a floor-contact line from a separate dark object sitting in the NE corner, given how dark the sampled colors are.

Testing the ratios across the sample points, they're not constant, so it's not a single straight edge on a constant-y plane. I also rule out a floor-level line since that ratio isn't constant either, and a constant-x plane doesn't fit since v should stay fixed but it varies across observations.

So this boundary must be a curve — maybe a silhouette of a rounded object. I should actually look at the image directly rather than reasoning purely from coordinates. Comparing color values, the (76,80,86) region matches the mass's top face tone seen in an earlier observation, so that patch likely IS the top face, while (22,24,25) is a much darker area, possibly a shadowed face pointing away from the light.

Reconsidering the geometry from the viewer's position looking east, the top face at that height should be visible below eye level, bounded by near and far edges — so I need to figure out whether (22,24,25) is actually the north face in shadow rather than something else entirely.

Checking the near top edge's predicted pixel position against the observed white-to-dark transition at u≈470, but my calculation gives v≈426, so there's a mismatch I need to resolve. The white region above the silhouette is the east wall, and I'm realizing the silhouette's upper boundary might actually correspond to the far edge of the top face rather than the near edge, since the mass extends away from the viewer to the south.

Wait, I think I had the orientation wrong—we're looking east, with the mass positioned both east and south of the camera. Its west face sits just 0.36 m ahead at x=2.456, so I'm recalculating the lateral pixel positions for its extent along y at that depth.

Working through this, the entire west face turns out to be off-frame to the right, but the north face becomes visible starting around u=511 pixels where x reaches about 2.562, so I'm computing where its top edge falls in the frame at those coordinates.

Comparing my computed top-edge values against the actual pixel data, I'm scanning columns to find where the dark region starts and stops — the top and bottom boundaries seem to shift with u, and I'm noting the color transitions to distinguish the dark surface from what lies below it.

That prediction is way off, so instead I'm solving directly for the boundary ratio from the data points: both u384/v441 and u416/v488 give (1.55-z)/d ≈ 1.4475, a consistent match, which tells me this is the actual north-face plane equation. Now I need to figure out what defines the top face's far edge along the east side to pin down the top height.

I'm wondering if maybe I've mislabeled which region is the north face versus the floor gap, and whether I should just look at the image directly again instead of continuing to guess numerically. If z=1.166 for the north face, that gives d≈0.265 for the depth term in this constraint.

Actually, if I test that against f159's measurement, y0 comes out to about 7.635 -- close to my earlier estimate of y≈7.60 for the north end, which is reassuring. But I also need to reconcile this with the possible degeneracy: the top-edge break in f159 near u≈32 and the silhouette edge in f162 near u≈246 both seemed to agree on y≈7.44, though I'm second-guessing whether the base run in f159 reaching u8 actually corresponds to y≈7.60 or a different value.

Now I'm second-guessing whether the base actually extends further north than the top edge, which would be odd. Maybe this isn't a single box at all -- perhaps there's a stepped structure where a lower section extends further north than the upper part, and the earlier v=438 measurement at u4 belongs to a separate base feature entirely.

Back-projecting that v=438 point gives coordinates around (2.88, 8.05), which sits beyond the x=2.456 boundary I'd been using. That suggests the gray mass could have an L-shaped footprint, with part of it extending further northeast than the main visible base.

This math alone won't resolve it — I should just look directly at obs_0164 and obs_0159 to see the actual layout.
